summary:
A visitor to Missouri stands under the national framework of the United States in every setting. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passports are issued only as M or F, so a trans visitor's documents may not match their presentation. Airport screening and visa decisions follow the same national rules, including the State Department's February 2025 announcement that trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', with a declaration of a gender other than sex assigned at birth capable of being treated as fraud and a permanent bar.

Missouri prohibits gender-affirming medical care for minors. The Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, Senate Bill 49, took effect on 28 August 2023 after a judge denied a preliminary injunction sought by the ACLU of Missouri, Lambda Legal and other counsel; the statute bars hormones and puberty blockers for under-18s unless the patient was already in treatment, and prohibits all transition-related surgery for minors.

The litigation has moved against the plaintiffs at every stage. Suit was filed on 25 July 2023 in Cole County Circuit Court by three families of transgender young people, medical providers, PFLAG National and GLMA. A Missouri judge upheld Senate Bill 49 on 25 November 2024, and on 13 January 2026 the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously upheld the ban on transition surgeries, cross-sex hormones and other gender-affirming care for minors, quoting the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that upheld Tennessee's similar law. Counsel have said they would appeal, and the case continues toward trial on the merits.

Correctional settings are separately restricted. An appropriations law signed by Governor Mike Kehoe and effective 2 July 2026 bars any state funds from paying for cross-sex hormones or gender-transition surgery for transgender people in Missouri prisons, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. Missouri thereby became the seventh state, and the second in 2026 after Oklahoma, to ban such care for inmates; Florida, Kentucky and North Carolina have near-identical statutes, while comparable measures in Idaho and Georgia were blocked by federal courts.

The SAFE Act also bars Missouri Medicaid from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, which reaches adults as well as minors, and exposes violating providers to licence revocation. The statute sunsets in 2027; lawmakers have signalled they want it made permanent, and a November 2026 ballot initiative seeks to ban such care indefinitely.
tangentialFactors:
Missouri's restrictions sit inside a national pattern rather than standing alone. The federal document rules, the visa policy for trans athletes and TSA screening procedures apply to a visitor in Missouri exactly as they apply in every other state, and the National Center for Transgender Equality's guidance describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers.

Facility use is regulated in a substantial number of states: bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with some jurisdictions treating trans bathroom use as a criminal offence in certain circumstances, while twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement has occurred, with a trans student arrested and handcuffed at the Florida state capitol in April 2025 in what civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Identity documents vary sharply by state. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, described by rights groups as a template other legislatures are following; the Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out state by state which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes and on what conditions.

Foreign governments have responded to the federal document and data rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens after detentions of European citizens over visa issues, and a national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four.

On the map's comparative scoring Missouri sits slightly below the national score of 0.36.
localsOnly:
Missouri residents face a care regime that has been upheld at every level and is moving toward permanence rather than invalidation. The SAFE Act has been in force since 28 August 2023, was upheld by a trial judge on 25 November 2024, and was unanimously upheld by the Missouri Supreme Court on 13 January 2026.

Medicaid coverage is barred for gender-affirming care at any age, so the funding restriction reaches adults as well as minors. Providers who violate the ban risk losing their Missouri medical licence and can be sued by patients up to 15 years after treatment.

Inccarcerated trans residents lost state funding for cross-sex hormones and transition surgery on 2 July 2026, with no taper plan for those already receiving care, making Missouri the seventh state to impose such a ban and the second in 2026.

Minors already in treatment when the SAFE Act took effect were exempted from the hormone and puberty-blocker prohibition, while transition-related surgery for minors is barred without such an exception.

Two pending routes could extend the restriction beyond its 2027 sunset: legislation to make the ban permanent, and a November 2026 ballot initiative to prohibit such care indefinitely.
